title: Ephesians 1:7–14
context: After the blessing of election (vv. 3–6, already live), Paul names redemption by Christ’s blood, the revealed mystery to sum up all things in Him, the inheritance predestined by God’s counsel, and the Spirit’s seal as guarantee.

voices.heading: Voices from both camps
voices.intro: On redemption by Christ’s blood, the mystery that unites all things in Him, the inheritance predestined by God’s counsel, and the Spirit’s seal, a few classic voices from each tradition.
voices.note: Quotations lightly abridged for length; wording follows standard English translations of the sources named.

arminian.quote: By whom we — Who believe. Have — From the moment we believe. Redemption — From the guilt and power of sin. Through his blood — Through what he hath done and suffered for us. According to the riches of his grace — According to the abundant overflowings of his free mercy and favour.
arminian.source: Explanatory Notes upon the New Testament (on Eph 1:7)

reformed.quote: By his death he has restored us to favor with the Father; and therefore we ought always to direct our minds to the blood of Christ, as the means by which we obtain divine grace. After mentioning that, through the blood of Christ, we obtain redemption, he immediately styles it the forgiveness of sins.

verses.text: In him we have our redemption through his blood, the forgiveness of our trespasses, according to the riches of his grace
verses.arminianNotes:
“In him we have our redemption through his blood, the forgiveness of our trespasses.” Wesley’s accent is pastoral and sequential: we who believe have, from the moment we believe, redemption from guilt and power, through what Christ has done and suffered.

Classical Arminians locate this “have” in living union entered by faith. The riches of grace are abundant overflowings of free mercy—sincerely offered, sufficient, received when sinners trust the blood. Forgiveness is not a distant idea; it is present pardon in Christ.
verses.reformedNotes:
Redemption is “in him,” through His blood, according to the riches of His grace. Calvin directs the mind to the blood as the means of restored favor: redemption is immediately styled the forgiveness of sins.

The cross actually obtains what it intends. Grace here is effectual for those united to Christ; forgiveness is blood-bought standing in the Son. The riches are the Father’s, already at work where He has placed His people.

verses.text: which he made to abound toward us in all wisdom and prudence,
verses.arminianNotes:
The grace of v. 7 is not stingy. God lavished it—poured it out—in all wisdom and prudence. The manner of giving matches the Giver: wise, insightful, abundant.

Lavish grace is enabling and sufficient. Wisdom and insight are given so that people may truly understand and respond. Overflowing mercy does not nullify the call to receive; it makes receiving possible and joyful.
verses.reformedNotes:
Lavished grace in all wisdom and prudence names both quantity and quality. God does not drip mercy; He pours it with perfect understanding of His purpose.

The wisdom is God’s, not ours as the source. What He lavishes He has planned; insight belongs first to the Counselor who redeems, then to those He enlightens in Christ.

verses.text: making known to us the mystery of his will, according to his good pleasure which he purposed in him
verses.arminianNotes:
God makes known the mystery of His will—revelation, not guesswork—according to His purpose set forth in Christ. The secret is now gospel: Christ is the place where God’s intention is displayed.

This is a purpose that is Christ-shaped and sincerely published. Making known implies hearers who can understand and believe. The mystery unveiled is an invitation into the purpose, not a locked list withheld from the church.
verses.reformedNotes:
The mystery of His will is made known according to His purpose, set forth in Christ. Revelation serves a prior purpose; Christ is where that purpose was always going.

“His will” and “His good pleasure” are not tentative. God discloses what He has determined to do in the Son. The church’s knowledge is gift, and the purpose stands in Christ whether or not every hearer welcomes it.

verses.text: to an administration of the fullness of the times, to sum up all things in Christ, the things in the heavens and the things on the earth, in him.
verses.arminianNotes:
The plan aims at the fullness of the times, to sum up all things in Christ, heaven and earth. Cosmic reconciliation is Christ-centered; nothing is finally left outside His summing-up.

In practice: “all things” displays the wide scope of Christ’s work and the sincere reach of the gospel. Uniting is not automatic universalism; it is God’s purpose in the Son, received by faith, awaiting the day’s completion.
verses.reformedNotes:
The administration of the fullness of time is to sum up all things in Christ—heaven and earth in Him. History has a Head; the end is not accident.

This is God’s plan, set forth in Christ, certain of fulfillment. Cosmic unity under the Son comforts the church: powers in heaven and earth are not rivals to the purpose already in motion.

verses.text: We were also assigned an inheritance in him, having been foreordained according to the purpose of him who does all things after the counsel of his will,
verses.arminianNotes:
We were also assigned an inheritance in him, having been foreordained according to the purpose of him who does all things after the counsel of his will. Inheritance belongs to those in Christ; predestination marks the destiny of the believing people.

Classical Arminians confess that God works all things and that His counsel is wise. They typically read the predestining here as the foreordained inheritance of those who are in the Son by grace-enabled faith—not an unconditional selection that would render the gospel offer insincere. Counsel does not cancel resistible grace.
verses.reformedNotes:
In Christ the people have obtained an inheritance because they were foreordained according to the purpose of him who does all things after the counsel of his will. The counsel is comprehensive; the predestination is the ground of the inheritance.

“All things” and “counsel of his will” name effectual sovereignty, not mere foresight. Those in Him were appointed to this inheritance by God’s purpose; faith comes from that counsel, not its condition. Assurance rests here: the will that works all things will not drop the inheritance.
verses.keyContrast: Arminian readings take “foreordained according to the purpose of him who does all things after the counsel of his will” as God’s appointed destiny for those in Christ by faith—counsel that enables and does not coerce. Reformed readings take the same counsel as God’s effectual purpose that works all things, including who obtains the inheritance; faith follows the counsel rather than founding it.

verses.text: to the end that we should be to the praise of his glory, we who had before hoped in Christ.
verses.arminianNotes:
The aim is doxology: we who had already hoped in Christ exist for the praise of His glory. Jewish believers (or the first generation) hoped first; hope is trust in the Messiah.

Hoping in Christ is a living act grace makes possible. Praise rises from people who have actually hoped—not from a purpose that bypasses response. Glory is magnified when hope is sincere and shared.
verses.reformedNotes:
The first to hope in Christ are appointed to the praise of His glory. Doxology is the end of predestination, not an afterthought.

Hope itself is located in God’s purpose (v. 11). Those who hoped first were not the authors of their privilege; they exist for His praise. Glory is safe because it rests on His counsel.

verses.text: In him you also, having heard the word of the truth, the Good News of your salvation—in whom, having also believed, you were sealed with the promised Holy Spirit,
verses.arminianNotes:
“In him you also, having heard the word of the truth, the Good News of your salvation—in whom, having also believed, you were sealed with the promised Holy Spirit.” The order on the page is pastoral: hearing the gospel, believing in Him, then sealing.

The note struck is a sequence. The word of truth is sincerely preached; faith is a response to enabling grace; the Spirit then seals those who have believed. Sealing confirms; it does not replace the call to trust the gospel when it is heard.
verses.reformedNotes:
Gentile readers (“you also”) are in Him: they heard the gospel, believed, and were sealed with the promised Spirit. The historical order of hearing and believing is the way God brings His people into possession of what He purposed.

Sealing is God’s mark and gift, not a human achievement. Hearing and believing are the appointed means; the Spirit’s seal is the Father’s own stamp on those united to Christ. Faith is authentic, and it is the fruit of effectual grace, not the cause of the union.
verses.keyContrast: Arminian readings typically underline the sequence—heard, believed, then sealed—as evidence that faith is a grace-enabled condition before the Spirit’s seal. Reformed readings typically treat hearing and believing as God’s appointed means, with the seal confirming those whom He has united to Christ by effectual grace; faith is the result, not the cause, of that union.

verses.text: who is a pledge of our inheritance, to the redemption of God’s own possession, to the praise of his glory.
verses.arminianNotes:
The Spirit is the guarantee—the down payment—of our inheritance, to the redemption of God’s own possession of it, again to the praise of His glory. Present seal pledges future fullness.

The down payment is true and generous. It assures those who remain in Christ by the faith the gospel first evoked. Glory will be praised when the inheritance is fully possessed; until then the seal both comforts and calls.
verses.reformedNotes:
The Spirit is God’s own pledge until the inheritance is fully possessed. The same doxology of v. 12 closes the unit: praise of His glory.

Comfort: a divine guarantee cannot finally fail. The Spirit who seals will see the people through to possession. Assurance is not arrogance; it is trust in the God whose counsel (v. 11) and pledge (v. 14) agree.
